newsitem.title: USA: Cities, GFOA warn House panel on Internet tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Cities, GFOA warn House panel on Internet tax bill.

text.p: State and local government groups told Congress Thursday that pending Internet tax legislation would have grave impacts for the nation's cities.
The National League of Cities and Government Finance Officers Association issued the warning in testimony before the House Judiciary subcommittee on commercial and administrative law.

The panel, chaired by Rep. George Gekas, R-Pa., is studying a fast-moving bill introduced by Rep. Christopher Cox, R-Calif., which calls for an indefinite moratorium on taxes that specifically target the Internet, such as taxes on World Wide Web access or online services.
Cities League spokesman Brian O'Neill, a Philadelphia council member, said his group and GFOA "strongly oppose" Cox's bill.

"An indefinite moratorium on state and local taxes on Internet or on-line services, as proposed, would put hundreds of state and local budgets in a deficit, create considerable budgetary problems for local governments, and lead to unfair competition in the marketplace," O'Neill said.
He conceded that a study of tax impacts on Internet growth is needed. But any moratorium should be imposed after the study is complete, not before, O'Neill said.
Gekas, however, warned that state and local taxes could strangle Internet development.

"Would our automobile industry have become the backbone of our economy for nearly half a century if, when the first 'Model T' rolled off the assembly line, toll booths were placed at every street corner and traffic light?" he asked.
Robert Holleyman, president of the Business Software Alliance, said the time is "ripe" for a moratorium.
He said Internet's success hinges on federal and state collaboration "before" states begin to depend on its tax revenues, not after.

"H.R. 1054 provides an opportunity to get it right the first time, and avoid the morass of inconsistent and incomprehensible taxation by the 30,000 localities that have the power to tax," Holleyman said, referring to Cox's bill.

The hearing is the second House session in a week on Cox's bill. Texas controller Wade Anderson warned the House Commerce subcommittee on telecommunications July 11 that Cox's bill would be "devastating" for states, localities, and their bondholders.
He said Texas, alone, would lose $1.25 billion annually in taxes if Internet measures offered by Cox in the House and Ron Wyden, D-Ore, in the Senate are enacted.
